verses.1: The saying is trustworthy: If anyone aspires to be an overseer, it means they desire a noble task.
verses.2: An overseer must be above reproach, married to one wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, and a teacher,
verses.3: not given to drinking, not violent, but gentle, not quarrelsome, and not a lover of money.
verses.4: They must manage their own household well, keeping their children under control with all dignity,
verses.5: for if someone does not know how to manage their own household, how will they care for God's assembly?
verses.6: They must not be a recent convert, or they might fall into condemnation and become pawns of the devil.
verses.7: Moreover, they must have a good reputation among outsiders, so they do not fall into disgrace or become a trap for the devil.
verses.8: In the same way, deacons must be dignified, not given to slander, not addicted to wine, and not greedy for money,
verses.9: keeping the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience.
verses.10: These people must also be tested first, and then serve if they prove themselves beyond reproach.
verses.11: In the same way, the women must be dignified, not slanderers, temperate, and faithful in everything.
verses.12: Deacons must be married to only one wife and must manage their children and their own households well.
verses.13: For those who serve well gain a good standing for themselves and great boldness in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.
verses.14: I am writing these things to you so that, if I delay coming, you will know how to conduct yourself in God's house,
verses.15: which is the assembly of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth.
verses.16: And this is acknowledged to be a great mystery of godliness: He who appeared in flesh, was vindicated in spirit, was seen by angels, was proclaimed among the nations, was believed in the world, and was taken up in glory.

notes:
Notes
- v. 16: The final verse is a poetic summary, often interpreted as a Christological hymn. The structure "He who appeared in flesh..." is rendered in a flowing English prose that respects the original's rhythm while maintaining clarity.
